name: Dark Indigo
lede: Dark indigo is the deepest blue a dyer could reach from the indigo vat, the color of burial cloths, chiefs' robes and rank; as a web swatch it has drifted to violet.

sections.title: Which dark indigo
sections.body:
There are two things called dark indigo. One is a dyer's term for deep blue cloth, the result of many dips in an indigo vat. The other is the swatch on this page, #1F0954, a web-era color from the 2010 xkcd survey [1]. The swatch is a dark violet: its hue angle is 308 degrees and its lightness only 10, and ISCC-NBS would call it a deep violet [1]. The nearest named colors are midnight blue and the family of [[dark-violet]] [1].

The dyed cloth is a darker, greyer blue than this chip, so the history below belongs to the dye, not to the swatch. Balfour-Paul, the main source for it, describes dark indigo-dyed robes as dark blue [2].

sections.title: Depth bought with dips
sections.body:
Dark indigo is an effect of repetition. Cloth lifted from the vat is greenish and turns blue in air, and each further dip deepens it, so the darkness of a garment records how much work and dye went into it [2]. Japanese dyers gave separate names to the blues from different numbers of immersions [3]. Eighteenth-century European dyers sorted indigo shades into thirteen grades, from milk blue and pearl blue up through queen's blue, garter blue and mazarine blue to the darkest, called infernal or navy blue [3].

The darkest grade explains a color word. Balfour-Paul notes that royal blue and navy blue left their indigo roots behind and entered common color language [3]. In Morocco, certain Berber shawls striped with indigo and black from other dyes were valued by the ratio of indigo to black, and dark indigo was often judged superior to black itself [3].

sections.title: Cost and rank
sections.body:
In middle Niger in 1865, by one historian's calculation, a dark indigo robe could cost as much as 10,000 cowries, about ninety times the daily subsistence of a man and his horse [4]. A tribal chief might wear a wide robe of narrow-strip cloth dipped up to forty times, and those who could not afford it beat indigo paste into white garments or rubbed indigo on the body to fake the tinge [4]. In Central Asia too, dark blues were preferred to light as a sign of wealth [5].

In medieval Mediterranean textile centers the coveted black called bruneta was made from woad and madder, and guild rules checked that the blue stage was dark enough before the madder bath [6]. Where black was concerned, the blue underneath did the work.

sections.title: Burial, mourning and marriage
sections.body:
Garments with dark indigo threads were used for important burials in ancient Egypt, Palestine, Mali and Peru, though nobody knows when indigo cloth first entered mourning rituals [7]. Mourning cloth is still dark indigo in Ghana and the Ivory Coast, and the Ebira of central Nigeria bury their dead in a cloth whose weft is entirely dark indigo yarn [8]. The Yoruba name olowududu for a prestige cloth refers to its very dark indigo color, *dudu* meaning black [9].

In the same vats came marriage and rank. A Javanese royal wedding cloth, the dodot, pairs a white diamond with a dark indigo ground to stand for earth and water, male and female, life and death [10]. In the 1930s Iban widows in Sarawak turned bright ceremonial wraps into mourning wear by dipping them in the indigo vat, which left light blue patterns on a very dark ground [11]. In nineteenth-century Persia, geometric weaves in dark indigo against ivory were called black and white [12].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body:
One painter used dark indigo as an underpainting. In Anthony van Dyck's *Charity* of about 1627-8 the ultramarine drapery lies over a dark indigo layer that tones the blue down, a restraint Ball sets against Titian's exuberance [13]. The word reaches back further: Gage reports that medieval Latin *saphirinus*, the sapphire-blue word, could describe opaque Frisian felts that were presumably dyed with a dark indigo [14].

We cannot see this layer under varnish. It is a fact from paint analysis, not from the picture's surface.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
As a painted surface the screen swatch is extremely rare. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of #1F0954 covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 7 works, all of them in shadow areas [15]. Five date from the 1700s and two from the 1800s, and four of the seven are British, a rate 23 times the archive's [15]. The largest, at 11 per cent, is the portrait of Miss Braddon by George Engleheart of 1775 [15].

The word has its own curve. In Google Books *indigo* peaks around 1830 and by 1940 stands at about a fifth of that height [16]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [15].

aka: navy blue (in the old dyer's grades)

questions.q: Why does the swatch called Dark Indigo not match dyed dark indigo cloth?
choices: The swatch is a dark violet, while the cloth is a darker, greyer blue
The cloth is dyed with a different plant
The swatch is lighter than the cloth
questions.answer: The swatch is a dark violet, while the cloth is a darker, greyer blue
